strengths: The paper addresses an important and difficult problem: temporally grounded reasoning over long videos, combining localization, verification, and question answering in one framework.
The Grounder is technically substantive, using a dedicated timestamp decoder, temporal feature pyramid, and multiple complementary training losses rather than generating timestamps as text.

The evaluation is unusually broad, covering 14 benchmarks across grounded VideoQA, temporal grounding, and general VideoQA. The reported results are consistently strong, especially for relatively small 2B and 7B backbones.
Ablations examine the individual roles, temporal pyramid, auxiliary loss, verifier design, and alternative role-integration strategies. These generally support the principal architectural choices.

Role-specific LoRA adapters offer a practical way to share a frozen backbone while retaining task specialization, and the comparison with separate model copies demonstrates a substantial model-memory advantage.
The manuscript is well organized, visually polished, and includes useful implementation details, prompts, dataset composition, and an interpretable qualitative example.
weaknesses: The main novelty is overstated. Dynamically switching role-specific LoRA adapters is conceptually straightforward, while the overall planner-grounder-verifier-answerer decomposition closely resembles existing modular and self-chained video agents.

The method is described as moment-level MCTS and inference-time search, but the presented algorithm is only a single top-N proposal-and-reranking procedure: it has no tree, iterative expansion, rollout, or standard MCTS selection mechanism.

Efficiency evidence is incomplete. Only model-weight memory is reported, although the system performs multiple video passes and verifies five candidates. Latency, FLOPs, peak activation memory, token/frame processing, and throughput comparisons are needed to substantiate computational-efficiency claims.

Some headline claims are misleading. On CG-Bench, the 2B model does not generally surpass GPT-4o: it is substantially worse in answer accuracy and worse in Acc@IoU, while exceeding it only on selected grounding metrics. The 7B model also remains worse in answer accuracy.

Evaluation fairness and data separation need clearer treatment. Training includes QVHighlights and TACoS, so results on those datasets are not zero-shot; planner training uses NExT-QA while evaluation includes its extension NExT-GQA. Exact video/question overlap checks and consistent labeling of fine-tuned versus zero-shot settings are missing.

The verifier only reranks fixed Grounder proposals and cannot actually correct their boundaries, despite repeated language suggesting refinement. Its gains therefore remain bounded by proposal recall, which is not reported.

The Planner supports only three predefined workflows, and its measured contribution is small: the main ablation shows an accuracy gain of only 0.8 points without uncertainty or significance analysis. This weakens the broader claim of flexible agentic planning.

Several technical and presentation details are insufficiently rigorous: Equation 3 appears to use h_r where the projected e_r is dimensionally expected, the contrastive negative set is unusual and underexplained, results lack variance across seeds, and training hardware, runtime, released code/checkpoints, and full split protocols are not provided.

The comparison between Chain-of-LoRA and All-Distributed establishes weight-memory equivalence but not an accuracy advantage; identical outputs are expected if the same independently trained adapters and backbone are used. Thus this experiment demonstrates an implementation optimization more than a learning contribution.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: temporally grounded reasoning over long videos, where explicit evidence localization can improve both accuracy and interpretability.

The proposed system is clearly decomposed into planner, grounder, verifier, and answerer roles. The timestamp decoder, temporal feature pyramid, and boundary-aware verifier are technically plausible components.

The empirical scope is broad, covering 14 benchmarks across grounded VideoQA, temporal grounding, and general VideoQA. Several results, particularly zero-shot grounding on Charades-STA and the verifier ablations, are promising.

The manuscript is generally well organized and supplies implementation settings, training-data summaries, prompts, and several component ablations. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_sample501_han_medium_20260920T175328Z/scratch/b4f209af2644406e8f5741ff2d9e4bdd/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: The central Chain-of-LoRA contribution is insufficiently novel and validated. The roles are trained separately and ordinary LoRA adapters are switched during inference; there is no learned chaining mechanism. The identical results of Chain-of-LoRA and All-Distributed are expected because they apparently execute the same role models, so Table 9 mainly demonstrates weight sharing rather than a substantive reasoning advance.

The paper describes its procedure as moment-level MCTS and inference-time search, but the actual method is one-shot generation of five candidates followed by independent binary reranking. It has no tree construction, iterative expansion, rollout, or value backup. This positioning materially overstates the method.

Several headline claims are contradicted or overstated by the tables. On CG-Bench, both VideoMind variants have substantially lower long-answer accuracy than GPT-4o; the 2B model also trails GPT-4o on Acc@IoU. Thus claims that the 2B model surpasses GPT-4o in accuracy or broadly outperforms it on grounded QA are unsupported.

Comparison protocols are not controlled sufficiently. The paper does not clearly align frame budgets, subtitles, prompts, evaluation splits, or inference compute across proprietary and open baselines. VideoMind repeatedly encodes the video and performs up to five verifier calls, yet only parameter memory is reported—no latency, FLOPs, throughput, or total token/frame processing—so the claimed computational efficiency is unsubstantiated.

Training/evaluation separation is inadequately documented. The grounder is trained on datasets later used for evaluation, including QVHighlights and TACoS, while the planner uses NExT-QA questions and is evaluated on the closely derived NExT-GQA benchmark. Exact split-level provenance and overlap checks are absent, making the zero-shot/generalization interpretation difficult to trust.

The key ablations do not convincingly isolate the full agent design. The planner improves ReXTime accuracy only marginally, the grounder and verifier yield small QA gains, and there is no comparison against simpler alternatives such as always grounding, confidence-based routing, shared multi-head adapters, or a conventional retrieval-and-reranking pipeline under matched compute.

The technical specification contains consequential inconsistencies. Equation 4 omits labels and the negative term of binary focal loss, so as written it pushes every frame toward foreground; Equation 3 uses hr after defining its projection er; the conditions under which regression losses apply are unspecified; and verifier “likelihoods” versus logits are ambiguous. These issues impede reproducibility.

Important evidence is missing: no variance or statistical significance, limited failure analysis, no study of sensitivity to the number of candidates or routing errors, and no breakdown showing whether gains come from more frames/repeated viewing rather than the proposed role structure. Code, checkpoints, and generated training annotations are also not committed for release.

The paper provides essentially no ethical discussion despite relying on large collections of web and egocentric video, automatically generated annotations, and potentially privacy-sensitive content. Dataset licensing, privacy, bias, and misuse considerations are not addressed.

strengths: VideoMind presents a clear and practically useful framework for long-video reasoning, decomposing the task into planning, temporal grounding, verification, and answering roles while sharing a single vision-language backbone.

The timestamp decoder, temporal feature pyramid, zoom-in verification, and role-specific LoRA adapters form a technically coherent design tailored to temporal evidence retrieval rather than merely applying textual chain-of-thought to video.

The empirical coverage is unusually broad: experiments span 14 benchmarks across grounded VideoQA, temporal grounding, and general VideoQA, with strong results from both 2B and 7B models. In particular, the temporal-grounding and grounded-QA improvements are substantial and often exceed much larger open models.

The ablations provide useful evidence for the timestamp-decoder components, feature-pyramid depth, verifier design, individual agent roles, and Chain-of-LoRA integration. The comparison with all-in-one and distributed implementations also supports the parameter-memory advantage of adapter switching.
The paper is generally well organized, visually clear, and includes prompts, training datasets, hyperparameters, and an explicit inference algorithm in the appendix.
weaknesses: The novelty is meaningful but somewhat incremental: role decomposition, candidate reranking, zoom-in processing, and switching task-specific LoRA adapters are established ideas. Their integration is effective, but the paper occasionally presents it as a more fundamental reasoning advance than the technical mechanism supports.

The discussion of inference-time search and MCTS is misleading. The implemented procedure appears to generate five candidates and independently rerank them with a verifier; it does not exhibit the tree expansion, iterative selection, or value propagation normally associated with MCTS.

The central efficiency claim is demonstrated mainly through resident GPU memory. VideoMind repeatedly processes the video through several roles and verifies five candidate segments, yet latency, total FLOPs, throughput, and end-to-end memory measurements are not reported. Moreover, a sequential distributed implementation need not keep four complete models resident simultaneously, making the 16.6 GB comparison an incomplete characterization of the practical tradeoff.

Some evaluation details are insufficiently specified. In particular, the model accepts at most 150 Grounder frames despite evaluating videos lasting up to an hour, but the sampling policy for such videos is unclear. Results also lack repeated runs, uncertainty estimates, training hardware, and a code or checkpoint availability statement.

The planner ablation is ambiguous: the 40%-grounding configuration reports improved mIoU even though samples routed directly to the Answerer seemingly produce no temporal interval. It is unclear whether mIoU is computed only on a selected subset, which would make it incomparable to the 100%-grounding rows. Algorithm 1 similarly returns a temporal output that is never explicitly assigned after candidate selection.

Several claims should be qualified. The 2B model does not surpass GPT-4o in CG-Bench answer accuracy, only in some grounding metrics; TACoS is included in pretraining and therefore should not be discussed as generalization; and the gains over closed models may reflect differing video sampling, subtitle use, or evaluation protocols.

There are minor technical and reproducibility issues, including an apparently incomplete focal-loss equation that omits the negative-class term, an unusual underspecified contrastive-negative definition, and no substantive discussion of dataset bias, privacy, or other ethical considerations associated with large-scale video training.

strengths: Addresses an important problem: interpretable long-video reasoning with explicit temporal evidence, rather than answer generation alone.
The unified planner-grounder-verifier-answerer pipeline is coherent, and the timestamp decoder, temporal feature pyramid, and zoom-in verifier are technically well motivated.

Evaluation is unusually broad, covering 15 benchmarks across grounded VideoQA, temporal grounding, and general VideoQA. Results are consistently strong, including notable gains from a relatively small 2B model.
The paper includes useful component ablations, alternative timestamp and verifier designs, error analysis, efficiency measurements, and tests with multiple open- and closed-source backbones.
Chain-of-LoRA provides a practical way to retain specialized roles while avoiding the memory cost of maintaining several complete models.

Implementation hyperparameters, training-data composition, prompts, metrics, and inference details are substantially documented, and the authors state that code, checkpoints, data, and logs will be released.
weaknesses: The main conceptual novelty is moderate. Dynamically switching among role-specific LoRA adapters is a natural engineering composition of established LoRA, agent, temporal-grounding, and verification ideas; the paper somewhat overstates it as a novel test-time scaling mechanism.

Some headline comparisons are not fully controlled: several closed-model results are taken from benchmark papers with different frame sampling, prompts, and settings. The controlled comparison uses only two 300-example subsets and reports neither uncertainty nor random seeds.

Training/evaluation separation needs clearer treatment. The system is trained on QVHighlights and TACoS and the planner uses NExT-QA, while evaluation includes QVHighlights, TACoS, and the closely related NExT-GQA. Although some tables acknowledge fine-tuning, claims of general or zero-shot capability could be delineated more carefully.

The core Chain-of-LoRA evidence is partly tautological: the distributed and Chain-of-LoRA variants use the same separately trained role modules and therefore obtain identical predictions. The experiments establish memory savings but do not deeply test adapter interaction, switching overhead, LoRA rank sensitivity, or alternatives such as adapter merging/routing.

Improvements in end-task QA attributable to the full agent are sometimes modest, while grounding gains are much larger. More controlled comparisons against the corresponding unmodified 7B backbone and stronger contemporary video models would better isolate the contribution.

Several technical details are underspecified or inconsistent: the focal-loss equation omits the negative-label term, Equation 3 appears to use the unprojected query representation instead of the defined projection, and target assignment/decoding for the multi-level timestamp head is not fully specified. Algorithm 1 also fails to assign the returned temporal interval explicitly and does not faithfully expose the planner's rephrased query.

The efficiency claim focuses mainly on peak memory. End-to-end compute, per-role latency, video decoding cost, training cost, and throughput across different video lengths are not comprehensively characterized.

The planner selects among only three predefined workflows, so the framing as a broadly flexible agent is stronger than what is demonstrated; multi-hop reasoning is handled through multiple proposals rather than genuinely iterative planning.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: combining temporal localization with evidence-grounded reasoning over long videos.
The timestamp decoder, temporal feature pyramid, zoom-in verifier, and role-specific workflow form a coherent system and produce strong results on a broad set of 15 benchmarks.
The evaluation includes multiple model sizes, component ablations, memory and latency measurements, error analysis, and comparisons with both specialist and general-purpose models.

Several results are compelling, particularly temporal grounding on Charades-STA and QVHighlights and grounded QA on NExT-GQA. The improvements from the verifier are consistent across several localization metrics.
Sharing one backbone while switching lightweight role-specific adapters offers a practically useful memory advantage over keeping several complete models.
weaknesses: The principal novelty is overstated. “Chain-of-LoRA” is essentially sequential activation of independently trained LoRA adapters; the equality between the distributed and Chain-of-LoRA results in Table 7 is largely expected because the underlying role modules are functionally the same. The paper does not demonstrate a new adapter-composition or joint-reasoning mechanism.

Some evaluation labels are misleading. The model is trained on QVHighlights and TACoS data but is presented with FT=false in places, while Table 11 only discloses co-training in its caption. This complicates comparisons against genuinely zero-shot methods and task-specific fine-tuning baselines.

There is a potentially important overlap concern: the planner is trained on NExT-QA and evaluated as part of the system on NExT-GQA, an extension derived from NExT-QA. The paper does not analyze shared videos or questions, making the reported planning and downstream generalization evidence difficult to interpret.

The planner supports only three predefined pipelines, with training labels largely determined by source-dataset question types. Its 93% held-out accuracy therefore measures recovery of these constructed labels rather than whether its plans are optimal. Comparisons against simple question-type routing, confidence-based routing, or an oracle planner are missing.

Several mathematical descriptions appear incorrect or incomplete: Equation 3 uses the unprojected hr despite a dimensional mismatch; the stated focal loss omits the negative-label term; and the contrastive-loss negative set excludes frames scoring above the selected positive, apparently leaving the hardest negatives unpenalized. It is unclear whether these are notation errors or implementation flaws.

The broad benchmark tables do not always provide controlled comparisons. Many closed-source results use settings inherited from benchmark papers, while the later controlled study uses only 300 randomly sampled examples per dataset and gives neither uncertainty estimates nor sampling seeds.

The strongest efficiency claim concerns model memory rather than end-to-end efficiency. The full pipeline repeatedly processes video segments and is slower than the cited reasoning baseline; the faster auto-planning result changes which samples receive the full procedure and does not report the corresponding accuracy tradeoff.

Reproducibility remains incomplete in the manuscript itself: role-training data construction, split and deduplication procedures, All-in-One baseline training details, frame-sampling policy for very long videos, and compute requirements are insufficiently specified. The abstract's resource link is also blank in the submitted PDF.

The limitations and ethics discussion is cursory given the use of large public video collections, synthetic annotations, and a system that could be applied to video surveillance or potentially sensitive temporal inference.

strengths: VideoMind presents a clear and practically useful framework for grounded video reasoning, combining planning, temporal localization, candidate verification, and answer generation in a coherent workflow.

The timestamp decoder is technically meaningful, and comparisons against alternative timestamp representations, temporal-pyramid ablations, and verifier variants provide concrete evidence for its design.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad, covering grounded VideoQA, temporal grounding, and general VideoQA across 15 benchmarks. Results are consistently strong, including substantial gains on several grounding benchmarks.

Chain-of-LoRA offers an effective engineering trade-off: it matches the performance of separately instantiated role models while reducing reported peak memory from 16.6 GB to 4.2 GB. Experiments across multiple backbone families further support portability.

The appendix provides useful implementation settings, prompts, efficiency measurements, error analyses, and experiments on multi-hop reasoning and closed-source models. The presentation and figures are generally clear.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is moderate. Switching among role-specific LoRA adapters is a natural application of existing adapter technology, while the temporal decoder and feature pyramid substantially reuse established temporal-localization designs. The paper sometimes overstates these elements as fundamentally novel reasoning or test-time-scaling mechanisms.

Some evaluation labels and comparisons are potentially misleading. TACoS is included in grounder and verifier training, yet Table 11 marks the method as not fine-tuned while acknowledging it was co-trained on that dataset; QVHighlights is likewise used for training. The paper should consistently distinguish target-dataset supervision from genuinely zero-shot transfer.

Several headline comparisons with proprietary models and prior methods use results imported from other papers under non-aligned settings. The controlled study addresses this concern only on two randomly downsampled 300-example subsets, without confidence intervals, repeated samples, or sufficient sampling details.

Important grounding details are underspecified, including target assignment across pyramid levels, construction and scoring of top-k proposals, regression decoding, and the complete classification objective. Equation 4 appears to show only the positive portion of binary focal loss. These omissions weaken reproducibility despite the stated intention to release code.

The evidence for the planner is limited: its 93% accuracy is measured on a random split of the same constructed training distribution with predetermined task-to-plan mappings. This does not establish robust planning under distribution shift or more flexible role sequences.

Efficiency claims focus on peak memory and comparison with one reasoning baseline. The multi-pass pipeline necessarily adds computation, but latency, FLOPs, and token/frame processing are not compared against the base model, answerer-only inference, or the all-in-one alternative. Claims of essentially no overhead should therefore be qualified.

The paper does not report uncertainty or statistical significance, and some gains on QA tasks are modest. Potential overlap between role-training sources and closely related evaluation datasets, especially NExT-QA versus NExT-GQA, should also be documented explicitly.
